strengths: The problem of policy rehearsing in offline reinforcement learning is interesting and challenging as an academic topic.
The description to the problem modeling and the methods is clear and generally easy-understanding.
The proposed method is well motivated by comprehensive preliminary theoretical analysis.
The experiment analysis is in-depth and insightful, which helps the readers better understand the effectiveness and underlying mechanism of the propose methods.
The method is similar to MAPLE but replaces the dynamics model generation process with a more directed procedure (RL on a custom reward vs learning an ensemble of models).
The reward used in the dynamics model generation process is well motivated by formal analysis of error bounds.
The different components of the method are analyzed/ablated.

The idea is novel unlike traditional model-based RL, this new idea suggests learning a bunch of transition models from reward function and termination functions, exempting the need for interaction data.

In terms of soundness, it proves empirically and theoretically that the transition models learned in this way can help warm up the policy and improve its performance when deployed in environments with diverse transition dynamics.

The ideas about the setting are novel and important, minimizing interaction with the environment as much as possible is an important problem in the RL community. Also, introducing rehearsal into RL is novel and enlightening.
The writing of Sec 3.2 is clear and solid, I have roughly read all the proofs, which are written quite clearly.
The proposed ReDM utilizes two novel terms for learning an imitated model, which is interesting and helpful.
weaknesses: The environments used in the experiments are still limited. I encourage to supplement more environments to demonstrate the applicability of your proposed method is possible. Otherwise, we may argue if the solution can only be effective on some specific kinds of tasks. Specifically, the current experiments are limited to relatively low-dimensional MuJoCo tasks. It is unclear how the method would scale to more complex environments with higher dimensional state and action spaces, where the hypothesis space for dynamics models is significantly larger. The paper should include experiments on more diverse and challenging environments to demonstrate the general applicability of the proposed method.

Considering the proposed method needs to train the new dynamics models and meta-policy simultaneously, the complexity of this method and the training stability/convegence are encouraged to be clarified and analyzed. The paper should provide a more detailed analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed method, including the number of parameters, training time, and memory requirements. Furthermore, the paper should discuss the convergence properties of the alternating training procedure for the dynamics models and meta-policy. It is important to analyze whether the training process is stable and converges to a good solution, or if it is prone to oscillations or divergence.

The assumed accessibility to the task reward function and initial state distribution is often unrealistic in the real applications. The paper assumes that the reward function and initial state distribution are known, which is a strong assumption that may not hold in many real-world scenarios. In practice, the reward function may be unknown or only partially known, and the initial state distribution may be difficult to estimate. The paper should discuss the limitations of this assumption and explore alternative approaches that do not rely on this assumption.
The method assumes access to a query-able reward/termination function and the initial state distribution, which may be unrealistic.
The method assumes dynamics can be easily parameterized and optimized with policy gradient, which may be unstable or inefficient for complex dynamics.
The method assumes random plans through the candidate dynamics models will achieve some non-zero reward, which may fail in sparse-reward or high-dimensional environments.
These assumptions make the method difficult to apply (if not impossible) in sparse-reward or high-dimensional (e.g., image-based) environments.
Limited scope of experiments: evaluations only on InvertedPendulum, MountainCar, Acrobot, HalfCheetah, and Hopper; missing Walker2d.

Experiments with interaction data only test random interaction data and relatively small amounts of data (200 and 5000 transitions); should also show comparison with varying optimality and amounts, including the full D4RL datasets.
No discussion of MAPLE in the related work section; similarities and differences should be addressed.
A brief mention of meta-learning should be included in related work as the proposed method uses similar concepts when optimizing for the adaptive policy.
Algorithm 1 does not say a lot about the method; it could be replaced by algorithms 5/6 from the appendix.
Figure 1 should use a more descriptive x-axis label like "Tasks".
Figure 3 needs a more descriptive caption that explains what "model loss" means here.
The locations of Figure 2 and Figure 3 should be switched.

The paper writing is not attractive; it contains too much tedious theoretical content and lacks an explanation for the rehearsal framework. Suggest moving some theoretical content to the appendix and adding at least one figure to explain the procedures of the new rehearsal framework.
No standard deviation is included for experiments in Table 1, and there is no error bar in Figure 7.
The term $D_{TV}$ should be explained in the main paper; it is strongly related to the main theorem but is currently undefined.
The meaning of relative performance is unclear; it is not explained whether it is calculated as the baseline performance minus something.
The axis "Number of models" in Figure 3 should be [0, 10, 20, 30, 40].
The connection between diversity and controlling $\epsilon_e$, $\epsilon_a$ is unclear; more explanation is needed about why $\epsilon_e$ can be controlled via diversity.
It is unclear why the proposed methods can help optimize the gap calculated in Theorem 3.3; a more direct connection between the objective in Sec 3.3 and the three errors in Theorem 3.3 is needed.
In experiments, providing results directly trained in the target environments as a reference would better show the results.
The paper lacks discussion of related works such as utilizing model-based methods for improving generalization [1-3] and finding diverse skills for unsupervised RL [4-6].
